title: The wounds (La Verna, 1224)
hook: near the end of his life, Francis receives the marks of the wounds of Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Greccio: a manger, an ox and a donkey. Your line was so they could see.

"I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body." Saint Paul wrote that to the Galatians, near the end of his letter. In another letter he lists beatings and a stoning, and some readers take the marks to be those scars, earned on the road. Now carry that sentence up a wooded mountain in Tuscany called La Verna, where Francis has gone with a few brothers to fast and pray, away from everyone. He is ill and worn out. What happens on that mountain gives Paul's word a new life: stigmata.
screen: `I BEAR THE MARKS.` → `A MOUNTAIN CALLED LA VERNA.` → `A WORN-OUT MAN AT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Thomas of Celano and Saint Bonaventure both tell it. While Francis prays, he sees a figure like a seraph, the angel of Isaiah's vision, with six wings, and between the wings a man fixed to a cross. Francis is torn between joy at the beauty of it and grief at the suffering, and he doesn't understand what he has seen. When the vision fades, the accounts say, the signs of nails appear in his hands and feet, and a wound opens in his side. Not paint, not a vision any more, but wounds he has to wrap. He didn't show them off. Celano says he hid them with great care, covering his hands, wearing something on his feet, and only a few close brothers knew while he lived. The marks were something given, and he guarded them like a secret between friends. The Church reads the stigmata not as a magic trick but as love made visible: Francis had spent years trying to follow Christ in poverty and humility, and his body, the tradition says, came to carry the shape of that love. Paul's word for the marks became the Church's word for this. Franciscans keep a feast of the stigmata of Saint Francis, and La Verna is still a place of prayer. Some readers take the accounts as a miracle exactly as told, and some ask what the brothers saw and how they described it. Either way, it's the story of a man marked by love.
screen: `A SERAPH, AND A MAN ON A CROSS.` · `NAILS, AND A WOUND IN THE SIDE.` · `HE HID THEM.` · `LOVE MADE VISIBLE.` · then, large: `I BEAR THE MARKS OF THE LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: Name one person to yourself who is sick, grieving, or hurting in a way you can see or one they've only told you about. Don't try to fix anything: if you pray, say their name to God and stay with it, and if you don't, keep them in your attention gently, the way you'd sit beside a hospital bed.
Stigmata. Paul's word for the marks of Jesus that he bore, and the Church's word for the wounds of Christ that Francis received on La Verna. Today's word.
Your line: marked by love. Next, a song from the end of his life. That's day eight hundred eight.

howItsDone: Franciscans keep a feast of the Stigmata of Saint Francis, and Franciscan friars care for the sanctuary at La Verna, where pilgrims still come to pray at the place of the vision.

chat.says: What does it mean that Saint Francis had the stigmata?
options: Accounts say Christ's wounds appeared on him: love made visible, the Church says.
He painted marks on his hands each Lent to remind people of the cross.
He showed his wounds in the town square, to prove his holiness to everyone.
chat.meaning: Celano and Bonaventure say wounds like Christ's appeared on Francis at La Verna; he hid them, and the Church reads them as love made visible.

notes: Year 1224 is in the index title only. The index hook says 'two years before his death'; the spoken text says only 'near the end of his life' and the hook line here was softened to match. Restore the two years only if confirmed in Celano (I, 94).
Galatians 6:17 linked to the beatings and stoning listed in 2 Corinthians 11:25 as one reading ('some readers'). Confirm.
Douay-Rheims Galatians 6:17 begins 'From henceforth let no man be troublesome to me; for I bear the marks...'; only the second clause is quoted. Confirm wording.

Vision details (seraph with six wings, a crucified man between the wings, joy and grief, not understanding), wounds in hands, feet and side, and the hiding: paraphrased from Celano and Bonaventure. Confirm.
'His eyes are failing' and 'his order has grown past anything he planned': confirm or cut.
Feast of the Stigmata of St. Francis (September 17) is kept by Franciscans and in some calendars; confirm 'the Church keeps a feast'.
Original: Greek στίγματα from Galatians 6:17; confirm accent and pronunciation.
